To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have isolated and characterized a novel integral membrane protein, kinectin (160-kD), which is an abundant kinesin-binding component on the ER and other organelles in neurons and non-neuronal cells.
a 160-kD membrane protein, called kinectin, has been isolated from brain microsomes that specifically binds kinesin.
we identified a major kinesins binding protein on the cytoplasmatic face of the ER and named it kinectin.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms by which organelle motility is regulated.
the molecular mechanism of microtubular-based organelle movement and the role of kinesin in the movement of organelles.
the molecular basis of organelle transport and the identification of the proteins involved in this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the 160-kDa protein is a kinesin-binding integral membrane protein of the ER.
kinectin is a major receptor for kinesin on ER.
kinectin is a major kinein-binding protein on the ER and that it is an integral protein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
kinectin is an integral membrane protein of ER that binds kinesin to ER membranes.
kinesin binds to the cytoplamix surface of microsomes via a 160-kD integral membrane protein, kinectin.
kinectin is an integral protein of the ER that is a major kinsin-binding protein and that it is a candidate for a membrane receptor in organelle transport.
The main takeaway from our work is that
kinesin binding to the ER membrane is not mediated by a soluble receptor but rather by a membrane receptor, kinectin.
kinesin is bound to the ER in vivo and that the binding is through an integral ER protein.
kinesin is a major component of the ER membrane in chick embryo fibrobasts and that kinectin is a major kinein-binding protein of this ER membrane.
